I would prioritize section boundaries, not a gap between every label and detail. The reported problem is difficulty locating sections; uniformly adding whitespace would preserve the ambiguous hierarchy while weakening the grouping that keeps a prerequisite beside its qualification.

Established constraints, from this consultation: retain the successful numbers/connectors/1–2–3 scan, author wording, persistent qualifications, and safe paragraph scrolling. Travis’s reported experience is poor section navigation; “vertical rhythm” is his tentative explanation, not approval of a particular remedy.

My inference: the layout gives different relationships nearly identical signals. Paragraph breaks, item transitions, and section transitions all have roughly the same spacing, while section headings compete with item labels in weight. That is a plausible explanation, not a verified visual diagnosis.

I recommend one bounded comparison with a simple hierarchy: no blank row between label and detail; retain the connector-only row between items; give genuine section transitions a larger break, starting with two blank rows rather than one. Use a thin, open horizontal rule as a section-level landmark, paired with existing section headings where present. Do not invent headings or put rules between every item. “Background and sources” should visibly belong to a different structural level from “02,” not merely be another bold line.

Keep every wrapped label line bold and aligned with the label’s text start; keep its detail normal-weight and immediately adjacent. In the donor-permission example, the mandatory-prerequisite qualification must read as part of that same numbered unit, not as a separate aside. If wrapping remains confusing, examine that alignment and weight distinction before inserting a gap.

Avoid boxes, enclosing borders, repeated full-width dividers, or extra padding around each item. Those would turn a connected sequence back into generic panels. Likewise, do not separate the persistent caveat from the title/scope it qualifies merely to make the top region look cleaner. The larger breaks belong between semantic sections, not between a statement and its constraint.

Compare the same JSON before and after at 72×35 and 80×24, without prose edits. Ask whether readers can locate the sequence and notes, distinguish a wrapped label from its detail, and still follow the numbered spine. Explicitly record the scrolling cost: the currently fitting case may stop fitting, and the procedure may require more scrolling. Check that new spacing and rule rows do not create orphaned headings, stranded labels, or unsafe scroll positions. Rules are landmarks, not substitutes for continuation disclosure.
